title: Define ship event endpoints before modeling berth and channel delays
problem: The berth-buffer model used the label departure delay for a quantity measured at handling completion, while the physical endpoint could instead be berth clearance, channel entry, a waiting place, or port exit. Owner feedback also identified weather, port/canal instructions, convoy order, route width, and capacity as omitted factors.
failure: A fixed-order single-berth example can be mistaken for a model of vessel navigation or port departure. It assumes bounded independent arrival and handling delays and does not identify where a vessel waits after service.
correction: Track separate times for handling completion C_i, berth release R_i, channel entry X_i, and the chosen port/holding endpoint. If a vessel can clear to a separate unconstrained holding area, channel slots do not feed back into berth-only feasibility. If the vessel remains at berth until its channel slot, channel delay blocks the next service. Shared pilots/tugs, limited anchorage, weather closure, convoy rules, and channel dimensions require explicit constraints.
transfer: Before optimizing a queue, name the physical event each deadline measures and where each item waits between stages. Test whether downstream resource delays feed back into upstream resource release. Distinguish a berth-only objective from total port-exit delay.
limits: This card captures owner-provided scope feedback and a two-vessel abstract illustration. It does not describe a specific port's regulations or establish a validated port schedule. The illustration is not a novelty claim; integrated berth/channel scheduling is established literature.
author: Owner domain feedback; TOTO formalization
